common_name: Conestoga Crape Myrtle (Early National Arboretum Lavender Tree-Form Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring or fall in full sun and well-drained soil; one of Dr. Donald Egolf's earliest US National Arboretum Lagerstroemia indica selections, released in 1967 alongside 'Catawba', 'Potomac', 'Powhatan', and 'Seminole', before the later indica x fauriei tribe-named hybrids were introduced.

directions: Conestoga grows into a vigorous, multi-trunked small tree that produces full, rounded panicles of lavender flowers in mid-summer on a fast-growing framework. As one of the National Arboretum's earliest pure Lagerstroemia indica releases, it predates the mildew-resistant indica x fauriei hybrids and can show more leaf spot in humid climates than its later tribe-named relatives, though it remains a reliable bloomer in open, sunny sites. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and allow it room to reach its mature tree-form size rather than crowding it against structures. Prune only to remove crossing or damaged wood in late winter, since flowers form on new growth.
sources: US National Arboretum, Lagerstroemia Cultivar Checklist
University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture Cooperative Extension

common_name: Midnight Magic Crape Myrtle (Compact Dark-Foliage Dark-Pink Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant in spring in full sun; part of the First Editions Magic series bred for compact habit, disease resistance, and strong foliage-to-flower color contrast, patented as PP25,925.

directions: Midnight Magic is the most compact member of the First Editions Magic series, holding darkest purple-to-burgundy foliage on a dense, rounded shrub that tops out well under most of its series siblings. Dark-pink flower clusters emerge from mid-summer through early fall, standing out clearly against the near-black leaves. Its small mature size makes it suitable for foundation plantings and mixed borders where a full-sized crape myrtle tree would be out of scale. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil, and deadhead spent panicles to encourage continued rebloom through the season.

common_name: Lunar Magic Crape Myrtle (Dark Foliage White-Flowered Reblooming Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant in spring in full sun; part of the First Editions Magic series, bred for disease-resistant foliage and a strong rebloom cycle, patented as PP30,360.

directions: Lunar Magic pairs dark, glossy purple-black to burgundy foliage with abundant clusters of shocking white flowers held on red stems, giving strong visual contrast on a rounded, multi-stemmed shrub. It reblooms readily through summer, sending up repeat flushes of bloom after light trimming of spent panicles rather than stalling out after a single early-season show. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil; the dark leaf color intensifies with more direct light exposure. Once established, it is drought tolerant and needs only routine late-winter pruning to remove dead or crossing wood.

common_name: Sunset Magic Crape Myrtle (Dark Foliage Cherry-Red Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant in spring in full sun; part of the First Editions Magic series, selected for leaf-spot and powdery-mildew resistance along with strong flower color on dark foliage.

directions: Sunset Magic covers itself in crinkly, cherry-red to deep-red flower clusters from midsummer onward, set against glossy, deep black-purple foliage that holds its rich color into late summer rather than fading to green. Its fast growth rate and compact-to-medium mature size make it adaptable to both shrub borders and small accent-tree training. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil for the deepest foliage color and heaviest bloom; deadhead spent clusters to push additional flushes of flower. It is bred for improved resistance to leaf spot and powdery mildew compared with older red-flowered crape myrtle cultivars.

common_name: Ruffled Red Magic Crape Myrtle (Green-Leaved Carnation-Flowered Red Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant in spring in full sun; part of the First Editions Magic series, patented as PP27,303, and notable within the series for retaining glossy green rather than dark purple foliage.

directions: Ruffled Red Magic stands apart from its Magic series siblings by keeping glossy dark green summer foliage instead of dark purple, turning orange-red only in fall, while still delivering the series' hallmark disease resistance. Its blooms are unusually frilled, carnation-like red flower clusters that glow against the green backdrop from midsummer through fall, reblooming after deadheading. It develops an upright but densely branched habit, reaching tree size at maturity with a compact-for-its-height canopy. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil and prune lightly in late winter to maintain an open branching structure.

common_name: Black Diamond Mystic Magenta Crape Myrtle (Dark Foliage Vibrant Magenta-Pink Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant in spring in full sun; foliage color and flower intensity in this Black Diamond series selection are both strongest in direct light.

directions: Mystic Magenta carries the Black Diamond series' near-black, charcoal-toned foliage and sets it off with abundant, luminous magenta-pink flower clusters from summer into fall. It forms a dense, rounded shrub-to-small-tree habit that works well as a specimen, informal hedge, or border accent where strong color contrast is wanted. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil; dark leaves show their deepest color and the flowers their brightest hue under full direct exposure. Once established it is drought tolerant and mildew resistant, needing only minimal structural pruning in late winter.
sources: Southern Living Plant Collection / Black Diamond series

common_name: Black Diamond Lavender Lace Crape Myrtle (Dark Foliage Pastel Purple Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant in spring in full sun; foliage color and flower intensity in this Black Diamond series selection are both strongest in direct light.

directions: Lavender Lace pairs the Black Diamond series' deep black-purple foliage with ruffled, papery pinkish-purple flower clusters accented by small yellow centers, giving a softer pastel look than the series' red and white siblings. Blooms can persist from summer right up to the first fall frost in many climates, on an upright, full-canopied shrub-to-small-tree form. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil for the darkest foliage and strongest bloom color; it tolerates heat and drought well once roots are established. Prune only to shape and remove dead or crossing wood in late winter, since flowers set on the current season's growth.
sources: Southern Living Plant Collection / Black Diamond series
